en.g: she; formerly an officially permitted Bokmål side form of hun (“she”), still common in dialectal and dialect-influenced writing

1000197.etyen:
Inherited from Middle Norwegian ho (“she”), from Old Norse hon (“she”), from Proto-Germanic *hēnō (“she”). The Middle Norwegian form developed through the regular loss of final -n in hon.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk ho, Icelandic hún, Faroese hon, Danish hun and Swedish hon (“she”).

en.g: fuck, screw; used to express rejection, contempt, or disregard for someone or something

1004037.etyen:
Borrowed from English fuck (“to fuck, copulate”), adapted with the Norwegian infinitive ending -e (“infinitive suffix”). The English verb is from Middle English *fukken (“to fuck, copulate”); its further origin is uncertain. A Germanic origin has been proposed, including possible connections with Old English *fuccian and Old Norse *fukka.
Compare the parallel borrowings Norwegian Nynorsk fucka and Swedish fucka (“to fuck up”).

en.g: a traditional hash from the Norwegian region of Østerdalen, made from finely chopped or ground meat—traditionally elk—and potatoes, often with onion and sometimes other vegetables
x: Det er for anledningen østerdalshakk, som besørges av Meskano.
For the occasion, Østerdalen hash will be served, provided by Meskano.
Lunsjen ville jeg tatt på Huldra, men middagen ville blitt Østerdalshakk på Taverna, med mandelpoteter selvfølgelig.
I would have had lunch at Huldra, but dinner would have been Østerdalen hash at Taverna, with almond potatoes, of course.

1004805.etyen:
From Østerdal (“Østerdalen”) + hakk (“hash; something chopped into small pieces”), with linking -s- (“interfix”), literally “Østerdalen hash”. The second element refers to the traditional preparation method, in which the meat was finely chopped with a broad knife on a chopping board; today it is generally ground.
The noun hakk is a verbal noun of hakke (“to chop”), from Low German hacken (“to chop”).
